drills.q: Is S3 still eventually consistent? What changed and when?
drills.a: No -- S3 has delivered strong read-after-write consistency automatically, for all requests, since December 2020, at no additional cost or performance penalty. A stale 'S3 is eventually consistent' answer is a pre-2020 fact.

drills.q: Does strong read-after-write consistency mean two concurrent writers to the same S3 key can't race?
drills.a: No -- it's still last-write-wins with no coordination between concurrent writers. Compare-and-swap semantics require explicitly using conditional writes (If-Match/If-None-Match).

drills.q: A team deletes objects from Glacier Deep Archive after 60 days to 'save money.' Does this reduce the bill below the minimum?
drills.a: No -- Glacier Deep Archive has a 180-day minimum storage duration; deleting at day 60 still bills for the remaining 120 days. Early deletion never reduces cost below any storage class's minimum-duration charge.

drills.q: What causes a 503 SlowDown error on a brand-new S3 prefix suddenly receiving high traffic, given the per-prefix rate limits are supposedly 3,500+/5,500+ requests per second?
drills.a: Those rates only apply once S3 has automatically partitioned the prefix based on sustained traffic. A cold prefix hit with a sudden burst can throttle before auto-partitioning catches up -- gradual ramp-up or pre-distributing initial load across multiple prefixes avoids this.

drills.q: Why does an S3 bill sometimes show storage costs with no matching objects visible in the console or aws s3 ls?
drills.a: Incomplete multipart uploads -- parts already uploaded from an upload that never completed (crash, network failure) are billed as storage indefinitely and are invisible to normal object listing. Use aws s3api list-multipart-uploads to find them, and a lifecycle rule with AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload to prevent recurrence.

drills.q: Design an S3 event consumer that's safe against both duplicate delivery and rapid-overwrite out-of-order delivery.
drills.a: Track the highest sequencer value processed per key (in a durable store like DynamoDB with a conditional write) and discard any incoming event whose sequencer is less than or equal to the stored value. This handles duplicates (equal sequencer, discard) and out-of-order arrivals (older sequencer arriving late, discard).

drills.q: What's the one edge case where S3 event notifications fail even the at-least-once guarantee?
drills.a: On rare occasions, notifications can be lost entirely, not just duplicated. Any pipeline where a missed event is unacceptable (billing, compliance archival) needs a periodic reconciliation job as a fallback, not reliance on events alone.

drills.q: What's the concrete performance difference between gp3 and gp2 that makes gp3 the default choice today?
drills.a: gp3 gives a flat 3,000 IOPS / 125 MiB/s baseline regardless of volume size, with extra IOPS/throughput provisionable independently at incremental cost. gp2 ties performance to volume size (3 IOPS/GiB, min 100) and relies on burst credits for small volumes, which degrade unpredictably once exhausted -- and gp3 is roughly 20% cheaper per GiB.

drills.q: A compliance team needs 7-year WORM retention that not even an admin can override. Governance or Compliance mode?
drills.a: Compliance mode -- it cannot be overridden by anyone, including the root account, until the retention period naturally expires. Governance mode can be overridden by a user with the bypass permission, which defeats a hard regulatory requirement.

drills.q: A presigned PUT URL was used to upload a 50GB file when only small images were expected. What's the fix?
drills.a: A bare presigned PUT URL has no content-type or size constraint -- whatever the client sends, S3 accepts. Use a presigned POST with an explicit policy document specifying content-length-range and content-type conditions, enforced server-side by S3.

drills.q: Two microservices need to pass large files between them. Why is mounting a shared EFS volume usually the wrong call?
drills.a: Unless there's a hard POSIX requirement (random-access read/write to the same file, directory locking, fsync guarantees), a shared filesystem reintroduces tight coupling and lock-contention between services. S3 with event notifications, or a proper queue, gives the same capability with better throughput scaling and no shared-mount failure domain.
